newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: DMG opens Argentina brokerage on bullish note.
newsitem.headline: DMG opens Argentina brokerage on bullish note.

text.p: Deutsche Morgan Grenfell took its first seat on a Latin American bourse in Argentina Tuesday, painting a bright picture of the local economy and predicting an upgrade in government debt by year-end.

"We believe the country has just started a new economic cycle of sustained growth which should continue at least until the year 2000," Daniel Tassan-Din, DMG head of equity research in Argentina said in a presentation marking the kickoff of its stock market seat.
"We expect by the end of this year or early 1998 a possible upgrade of Argentine debt (by Moody's and Standard & Poor's)," he said.
Moody's and S&P currently have a B1 rating and a BB- rating, respectively, on Argentina's long-term foreign currency denominated debt.
DMG, whose parent company is Deutsche Bank, chose Argentina as its first stop in terms of establishing its trading presence in Latin America.
It already has sales and research offices in eight Latin American countries and will open brokerages in Brazil late March and Mexico early April.

Tassan-Din predicted that the Argentine economy, shielded by low international interest rates and bolstered by higher exports, investments and consumption, would grow 4.9 percent in 1997 against an estimated Latin American average of 4.4 percent.
Gross domestic product rose 4.4 percent last year against a 4.6 percent drop in 1995 in the aftermath of the shock Mexican devaluation.

"One of the most overlooked aspects when you consider Argentina's long-term economic growth prospects is the positive impact of structural reforms that have been implemented since 1991," Tassan-Din said.

He noted only Chile has completed its structural reforms but Argentina's were also advanced. "This transformation has not been fully reflected in market valuations, and in the next two years this should allow for higher-than-expected returns on the equity market."

The analyst said DMG's 12-month target for the leading MerVal stock index was 860, based on several factors including a U.S. long bond yield of 6.5 percent and 16 percent earnings per share growth. For the year 2000 it sees the MerVal at 1200, implying a 19 percent annual compound growth rate.
The MerVal closed at 759.17 Monday at a high of nearly five years.

Tassan-Din said Argentina's financial needs for 1997 have been almost 40 percent secured, adding, "We believe that the current environment of strong liquidity in the domestic and international markets should continue to bode well for the country."

Jonathan Beatson-Hird, New-York based head of DMG's Latin American Equities Operations, said at Tuesday's launch that a local presence and local clients in countries like Argentina were essential to boost DMG's Latin American operations.
"We are eager to be able to take part in what is a very dynamic and exciting future for Argentina," said Beatson-Hird.

"The economic background in Latin America hasn't been this good for 20 years, which means we have a great outlook," said Stuart Parkinson, DMG's chief economist for emerging markets based in London. "Argentina is at the forefront of the economic change that's occured, so it should benefit very much in the coming few years."
